<div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

Rust lets a program call a method without knowing the exact kind of object receiving the call. To do that, the compiler builds a small table of addresses—called a *vtable*—that tells the program where each method’s code lives. In this bug, Rust 1.98.0 built a table with a zero where a method address should have been. When a proxy server written in safe Rust called that method, it jumped to address zero and crashed.

The proxy was supposed to handle a failed connection by returning “502 Bad Gateway” and continuing to run. That is what happened with Rust 1.97.1 and with a later nightly compiler. With 1.98.0, the same source code could instead crash while handling the request. The reporter traced the crash to a boxed asynchronous service: a component whose precise type had been hidden so it could be called through the vtable. The compiler had generated the caller, but had wrongly left out the callable method’s entry.

Why would it leave a method out? Before putting a method in a vtable, the compiler checks whether the conditions required for that method could possibly be satisfied. If it concludes they cannot, it may leave the slot vacant. Here, that conclusion was wrong. The conditions involved an *opaque type*: a type whose concrete identity is deliberately hidden at one stage of compilation but is available at another. Rust’s trait solver—the part of the compiler that reasons about which types meet which requirements—needed to reconsider its answer using that later information.

Two compiler changes had landed on opposite sides of the cutoff for the 1.98 release. The first changed how the solver handled certain type aliases and exposed this case. The second corrected when the solver repeats a check in its original typing mode after encountering opaque types. Without the correction, two reasons for repeating the check could be combined in a way that made the solver skip the repeat. It then treated a usable method as impossible, producing the empty vtable slot.

This was a compiler bug, not misuse of an unsafe feature by the application. Although the most obvious result was a crash, an invalid method address makes the program’s behavior undefined; investigators also found an optimized example that changed behavior without simply crashing.

The community reduced the large proxy example to a short, self-contained reproduction and identified the relevant compiler changes. Rust’s maintainers backported the solver correction, added a regression test that actually calls through the affected vtable, and released it in **Rust 1.98.1**. The issue was closed after that release.

This was a Rust compiler bug that made some perfectly valid programs crash, even though the programs were written in safe Rust. That is serious because one of Rust’s main promises is that safe Rust should not be able to cause low-level memory errors such as jumping to address zero.

The affected program used a common Rust pattern: storing a service behind a “boxed” interface. Imagine you have many different kinds of machines, but you put them all behind the same front panel with one button labeled “serve.” The rest of the program does not need to know which machine is behind the panel; it just presses the button.

At the machine-code level, Rust implements this kind of “front panel” using a small table of function pointers called a vtable. The table says, in effect: “to destroy this object, call this function; to ask its size, use this value; to call its `serve` method, jump to this address.” When the program invokes the boxed service, it looks up the right function address in the vtable and jumps there.

In Rust 1.98.0, the compiler sometimes produced a vtable where the method slot was empty: it contained zero instead of the address of the real method. So when the program tried to call the service, it loaded the zero address and jumped to it. On macOS this showed up as a segmentation fault with the program counter exactly at zero.

The original report came from the Rama project, a Rust networking framework. Their proxy example worked on Rust 1.97.1, crashed on Rust 1.98.0, and worked again on a later nightly compiler. That strongly suggested a compiler regression rather than an application bug.

The deeper cause involved Rust’s trait solver, the part of the compiler that reasons about whether a type satisfies some set of requirements. In this case, the compiler was trying to decide whether a particular method should exist in the vtable. Because of a subtle interaction involving opaque types — types whose exact identity is hidden, such as those created by `async fn` or `impl Trait` — the compiler incorrectly concluded that the method’s requirements were impossible to satisfy.

Once it believed the method was impossible, it treated the vtable slot as “vacant.” But the program could in fact reach that method through normal safe Rust code. So the compiler’s reasoning and the generated executable disagreed, producing undefined behavior.

The regression was traced to Rust pull request #156742, which changed how the newer trait solver handles certain “rigid” aliases. A later pull request, #158993, had already fixed the underlying issue on nightly and beta by making the solver retry certain checks in the correct typing mode when opaque types are involved. However, Rust 1.98.0 was released in the gap between the regression and that fix.

The fix was therefore to backport #158993 to the stable 1.98 branch. That happened in pull request #161555, which became Rust 1.98.1. The patch changed the solver so that when it encounters this particular combination of hidden/opaque type information during later compiler phases, it reruns the check in the original mode instead of accepting the wrong “impossible” result.

Rust 1.98.1 also added regression tests, including a small minimized example, to ensure the compiler no longer emits a vtable with a missing method slot in this situation.

In short: Rust 1.98.0’s compiler sometimes convinced itself that a real method could never be called, left its vtable entry blank, and generated a crashing binary. Rust 1.98.1 fixed the compiler’s reasoning so the method is recognized and emitted correctly.

<div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

This was a **Rust compiler miscompilation in Rust 1.98.0**. Safe Rust code could be compiled into a binary containing an invalid trait-object vtable, where a method pointer slot was `0`. Calling that method through dynamic dispatch then jumped to address `0`, causing a segfault — or, under optimization, potentially worse undefined behavior.

It was fixed in **Rust 1.98.1**.

---

## The short version

Rust trait objects like `dyn Trait` are implemented using a pointer to data plus a pointer to a **vtable**.

A vtable contains entries like:

```text
drop glue
size
alignment
method_1 pointer
method_2 pointer
...
```

In this bug, Rust 1.98.0 generated a vtable where the first method entry was effectively:

```text
method_1 pointer = 0x0000000000000000
```

Then ordinary safe Rust code did dynamic dispatch:

```rust
trait_object.method()
```

which compiled roughly to:

```text
load method pointer from vtable
call method pointer
```

But the loaded pointer was zero, so the program jumped to address zero and crashed.

That is a compiler soundness bug: safe Rust should not be able to produce undefined behavior like this.

---

## What kind of code triggered it?

The original report involved Rama’s boxed async service abstraction, roughly of this shape:

```rust
trait Service<Input> {
    type Output;
    type Error;

    fn serve(&self, input: Input) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Self::Output, Self::Error>>;
}
```

Because `async fn` in traits and `impl Future` can be hard to make directly object-safe, Rama used a common erasure pattern:

```rust
trait DynService<Input> {
    type Output;
    type Error;

    fn serve_box(
        &self,
        input: Input,
    ) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = Result<Self::Output, Self::Error>> + Send + '_>>;
}

impl<Input, T> DynService<Input> for T
where
    T: Service<Input>,
{
    type Output = T::Output;
    type Error = T::Error;

    fn serve_box(&self, input: Input) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = _> + Send + '_>> {
        Box::pin(self.serve(input))
    }
}
```

Then a boxed service stored something like:

```rust
Arc<dyn DynService<Input, Output = O, Error = E> + Send + Sync>
```

This is a normal pattern: erase the concrete service type behind a trait object, then call through the vtable.

In Rust 1.98.0, for a sufficiently complex combination of:

- generic trait impls,
- associated types,
- opaque types such as `impl Trait`,
- async functions / futures,
- dynamic dispatch,
- and nested trait bounds,

the compiler incorrectly concluded that one of the trait-object method implementations was impossible or unavailable.

So it emitted a vtable with a **vacant method slot**.

---

## The minimized reproducer

The issue was eventually reduced to a surprisingly small example:

```rust
use std::marker::PhantomData;

struct MyError;

trait StreamingBody {
    type BodyError;
}

struct Body;

impl StreamingBody for Body {
    type BodyError = MyError;
}

trait Service {
    type Output;
}

struct HttpClientService;

impl Service for HttpClientService {
    type Output = Body;
}

trait Trait {
    fn method(&self);
}

impl<F, R, ResBody> Trait for (F, PhantomData<R>)
where
    F: Fn() -> R,
    HttpClientService: Service<Output = ResBody>,
    ResBody: StreamingBody<BodyError: Sized>,
{
    fn method(&self) {}
}

fn inspect_websocket_message() -> impl Sized {
    || {}
}

fn main() {
    (&(inspect_websocket_message, PhantomData) as &dyn Trait).method();
    println!("done");
}
```

This is not doing anything unsafe. It merely coerces a value to `&dyn Trait` and calls `method`.

But on the affected compiler, the generated vtable could contain a missing/null method entry.

A previous version of the minimized reproducer used:

```rust
async fn inspect_websocket_message() {}
```

The async function was originally thought to be essential, but it turned out that an `impl Trait` return type was enough to trigger the underlying problem.

---

## Why did the compiler put a vacant slot in the vtable?

Rust sometimes has to decide whether an impl can apply.

For example, this impl:

```rust
impl<F, R, ResBody> Trait for (F, PhantomData<R>)
where
    F: Fn() -> R,
    HttpClientService: Service<Output = ResBody>,
    ResBody: StreamingBody<BodyError: Sized>,
{
    fn method(&self) {}
}
```

is only valid if its where-clauses are satisfiable.

When building a vtable for `dyn Trait`, rustc has logic that asks, in effect:

> Is this method actually callable for this concrete type under the required predicates?

If the compiler decides “no, these predicates are impossible,” it can mark the vtable entry as vacant. Internally this corresponds to something like `VtblEntry::Vacant`.

That is valid for truly impossible methods. For example, some trait-object methods cannot be called because of `Self: Sized` bounds. Those should not get callable vtable entries.

The bug was that Rust 1.98.0 incorrectly decided that a valid method was impossible.

So instead of producing:

```text
vtable:
  drop
  size
  align
  pointer to <Concrete as Trait>::method
```

it produced approximately:

```text
vtable:
  drop
  size
  align
  0
```

Then safe code dispatched through that zero pointer.

---

## The role of the “next trait solver”

The root cause was in Rust’s newer trait solver machinery.

Even though the “next solver” is not fully used everywhere on stable Rust, parts of rustc already rely on it internally. In particular, this bug involved the `impossible_predicates` logic, which asks whether a set of trait bounds can ever hold.

That logic used next-solver behavior, and Rust 1.98.0 had a regression involving:

- opaque types, such as `impl Trait`,
- different compiler “typing modes”,
- post-analysis/codegen-time trait evaluation,
- and whether obligations should be rerun in a more appropriate typing mode.

The relevant chain was:

1. PR `#156742` added “rigid alias” machinery to the new trait solver.
2. That introduced or exposed a bug where certain goals involving opaque types were not reevaluated correctly in codegen/post-analysis mode.
3. As a result, `impossible_predicates` could incorrectly decide that valid predicates were impossible.
4. Vtable construction believed a trait method was uncallable.
5. Rust emitted a vacant vtable slot.
6. Dynamic dispatch called through that vacant slot.
7. The program segfaulted or exhibited UB.

The fix had already landed on nightly/beta in PR `#158993`, but it missed the 1.98.0 stable cutoff.

That is why:

- Rust 1.97.1 worked,
- Rust 1.98.0 was broken,
- nightly shortly after the fix worked,
- Rust 1.99 beta worked,
- and Rust 1.98.1 fixed stable.

---

## Why was this especially serious?

A compiler crash would have been annoying but relatively contained.

This was worse: rustc successfully compiled the program, but produced a bad binary.

The bad binary contained undefined behavior reachable from safe Rust. The common symptom was a jump to address zero:

```text
SIGSEGV at 0x0000000000000000
```

But undefined behavior is not limited to clean crashes. Commenters observed cases involving:

- `SIGSEGV`,
- `SIGILL`,
- strange panic behavior,
- and optimized builds where behavior changed without simply crashing.

That is why this warranted a patch release.

---

## Why did the workaround help?

One workaround replaced this:

```rust
Arc<dyn DynService<Input, Output = Output, Error = Error> + Send + Sync>
```

with a manually stored function pointer:

```rust
struct BoxService<Input, Output, Error> {
    inner: Arc<dyn Any + Send + Sync + 'static>,
    serve: for<'a> fn(
        &'a dyn Any,
        Input,
    ) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = Result<Output, Error>> + Send + 'a>>,
}
```

Instead of relying on a compiler-generated trait-object vtable for `DynService`, it stored the dispatch function explicitly.

So the call became more like:

```rust
(self.serve)(self.inner.as_ref(), input)
```

rather than:

```rust
self.inner.serve_box(input)
```

That avoided the broken vtable-generation path.

Another workaround wrapped the responder in an erased closure:

```rust
Arc<dyn Fn(Request) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = _> + Send>> + Send + Sync>
```

Again, this shifted the code away from the specific trait/vtable/predicate combination that triggered the compiler bug.

But these were only workarounds. The original code was not doing something inherently wrong.

---

## Final resolution

The fix was backported in PR `#161555`, released as **Rust 1.98.1**.

The release notes included:

> rustc: fix miscompilation in generating vtables

The issue was then closed once 1.98.1 shipped.

---

## Practical takeaway

If you used Rust 1.98.0 and had code involving complex trait bounds, `impl Trait`, async services, or dynamic dispatch, you should avoid 1.98.0 and update to at least:

```text
Rust 1.98.1
```

This was a real stable compiler bug, not user error.

The affected code was safe Rust, and the crash came from rustc incorrectly generating a trait-object vtable with a missing method pointer.

In Rust 1.98.0, the compiler sometimes generated a vtable where one of those contact-list entries was empty: it contained zero instead of the address of the method. These are like sealed boxes: outside code knows what promises the type makes, but not its exact shape. The compiler sometimes analyzes code in a mode where those boxes remain sealed, and later in a mode where their contents are known.

The bug was that, in one combined situation involving opaque types and inference placeholders, the compiler should have re-run a trait check in the more precise mode, but did not. The fix was small but important: when this combined opaque-type condition appears during later compiler phases, Rust now re-runs the trait check in the original, more appropriate typing mode. That change had already landed on nightly, which is why nightly builds no longer reproduced the crash. It was then backported to stable and released as Rust 1.98.1, along with regression tests ensuring that the compiler no longer emits a null vtable entry for this case.

<div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

Short version: **Rust 1.98.0 sometimes built an invalid trait-object vtable**. It put `0` in the slot where a real method function pointer should have gone. Later, perfectly safe Rust did dynamic dispatch through that slot, so the CPU jumped to address `0`, causing a segfault.

This was a compiler miscompilation, not a Rama bug.

---

## What the program was doing

Rama had a boxed async service abstraction roughly like this:

```rust
trait DynService<Input> {
    fn serve_box(&self, input: Input) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ...> + Send + '_>>;
}

impl<Input, T> DynService<Input> for T
where
    T: Service<Input>,
{
    fn serve_box(&self, input: Input) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ...> + Send + '_>> {
        Box::pin(self.serve(input))
    }
}

struct BoxService<Input, Output, Error> {
    inner: Arc<dyn DynService<Input, Output = Output, Error = Error> + Send + Sync>,
}
```

So calling the service goes through a trait object:

```rust
self.inner.serve_box(input)
```

A Rust trait object is represented like:

```text
data pointer  ---> actual concrete value
vtable pointer ---> table of function pointers and metadata
```

The vtable contains entries like:

```text
drop function
size
alignment
method 1 function pointer
method 2 function pointer
...
```

On a 64-bit target, the first method pointer is often at offset `0x18`, after the three metadata words.

In the bad Rust 1.98.0 build, the vtable looked conceptually like:

```text
drop      = valid
size      = valid
align     = valid
serve_box = 0
```

Then the generated code did the normal dynamic-dispatch sequence:

```text
load method pointer from vtable + 0x18
call it
```

But the loaded method pointer was `0`, so the process jumped to address zero and crashed.

---

## Why would rustc ever put zero in a vtable?

Rustc has an internal notion of a “vacant” vtable slot, represented by something like `VtblEntry::Vacant`.

That is legitimate only when the compiler knows that a method cannot actually be called for that trait object. For example, some trait methods have extra `where Self: Sized`-style restrictions and are intentionally not dynamically dispatchable.

But here the method was callable. The type checked. The impl existed. Safe Rust later dispatched through it.

The compiler had incorrectly concluded that the method’s predicates were impossible, so it emitted a vacant slot instead of the real method pointer.

That is the core bug.

---

## The real root cause: a trait-solver mistake involving opaque types

The minimized reproducer was much smaller than Rama and looked roughly like this:

```rust
trait StreamingBody {
    type BodyError;
}

struct Body;
impl StreamingBody for Body {
    type BodyError = MyError;
}

trait Service {
    type Output;
}

struct HttpClientService;
impl Service for HttpClientService {
    type Output = Body;
}

trait Trait {
    fn method(&self);
}

impl<F, R, ResBody> Trait for (F, PhantomData<R>)
where
    F: Fn() -> R,
    HttpClientService: Service<Output = ResBody>,
    ResBody: StreamingBody<BodyError: Sized>,
{
    fn method(&self) {}
}

fn inspect_websocket_message() -> impl Sized {}

fn main() {
    (&(inspect_websocket_message, PhantomData) as &dyn Trait).method();
}
```

The impl is valid:

- `inspect_websocket_message` is a function.
- It returns some opaque type, written `impl Sized`.
- `HttpClientService::Output` is `Body`.
- `Body` implements `StreamingBody`.
- `Body::BodyError` is `MyError`, which is `Sized`.

So the trait object should have a valid `method` pointer.

Rust 1.98.0’s trait solver got confused by the combination of:

1. a function returning an opaque type, such as `impl Sized` or the hidden future from an `async fn`,
2. associated type normalization, such as:

   ```rust
   HttpClientService: Service<Output = ResBody>
   ```

3. another bound on the normalized associated type:

   ```rust
   ResBody: StreamingBody<BodyError: Sized>
   ```

4. vtable generation asking “are this impl’s predicates impossible?”

The answer should have been “no, they are possible and satisfied.”

Rust 1.98.0 sometimes answered “yes, impossible.”

That bad answer caused rustc to generate a vacant vtable entry.

---

## Why async appeared to matter

The original Rama code involved async services. An `async fn` in Rust secretly returns an opaque future type:

```rust
async fn foo() -> T
```

is morally like:

```rust
fn foo() -> impl Future<Output = T>
```

So async was not magical here. It was one common way to introduce an opaque return type.

The minimized reproducer showed that this also failed with:

```rust
fn inspect_websocket_message() -> impl Sized {}
```

So the essential trigger was not async itself, but **opaque return types** interacting with trait solving and associated type predicates.

---

## Why Rust 1.97 worked, 1.98 broke, and nightly worked again

The regression came from rust-lang/rust#156742, which added “rigid alias” handling to the next-generation trait solver.

A type alias here means things like:

```rust
<T as Trait>::Assoc
```

or an opaque type like:

```rust
impl Future<Output = T>
```

The compiler sometimes keeps these aliases “rigid” instead of immediately normalizing/revealing them. That is useful, but only inside the right compiler typing environment.

Rustc has different modes/phases, such as type checking, post-analysis, and code generation. Opaque types may be treated differently in those phases. If the solver sees an opaque type in a later phase, it may need to rerun the query in the original mode.

Rust 1.98.0 missed one such rerun case. Internally, a combined condition named approximately:

```text
OpaqueInStorageOrAnyOpaqueHasInferAsHidden
```

failed to trigger a rerun during post-analysis/codegen.

So a temporary “I cannot prove this in this mode” situation became a final “this predicate is impossible.”

That false “impossible” result poisoned vtable generation.

The fix, rust-lang/rust#158993, changed that case from “do not rerun” to “rerun.” It was already present in later nightly/beta compilers, but it missed the Rust 1.98.0 stable cutoff. It was then backported in Rust 1.98.1.

---

## Why the crash could vary

The most obvious symptom was:

```text
SIGSEGV at address 0
```

because the program literally called through a null function pointer.

But once generated code contains an impossible/null function call, optimizers may make further assumptions. So other symptoms are possible: SIGILL, odd panics, or wrong behavior under optimization.

That does not mean the user program had undefined behavior in source Rust. It means the compiler emitted bad machine code.

---

## Why the workaround helped

The Rama workaround changed the dynamic-dispatch boundary.

Instead of storing the complex service behind the problematic custom trait-object vtable, it used either:

```rust
Arc<dyn Fn(Request) -> BoxFuture<...>>
```

or stored:

```rust
Arc<dyn Any + Send + Sync>
```

plus a separate monomorphic function pointer.

That avoided asking rustc to build the particular bad vtable entry for the complex `DynService` impl. The underlying service logic was still fine; the workaround just avoided the compiler bug’s trigger shape.

---

## Bottom line

Rust 1.98.0 had a soundness-affecting compiler bug:

> it could incorrectly decide that a valid trait impl’s predicates were impossible during vtable construction, emit a null method slot, and later safe Rust would dynamically dispatch through that null slot.

It was fixed in Rust 1.98.1 by backporting the trait-solver rerun fix. The correct practical answer is: **use Rust 1.98.1 or newer**.

<div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

A Rust user hit a rare but serious compiler bug in Rust 1.98: a program written in *safe* Rust (code that is supposed to be protected from memory-safety crashes) sometimes crashed at runtime with a segmentation fault. The crash happened when the program tried to call a “boxed” service—roughly, an object stored behind a generic “handle” that lets you call different implementations through the same interface.

Under the hood, when Rust uses this kind of “call through an interface,” it relies on a small table of function pointers, called a *vtable* (virtual method table). You can think of a vtable like a remote control: pressing button 1 calls the correct function for that particular device. The vtable must contain valid addresses for each method. In Rust 1.98, the compiler sometimes generated a vtable where one of those method entries was *zero* (a null pointer). Then, when the program pressed that button (called the method), the CPU tried to jump to address 0—an invalid address—causing an immediate crash (SIGSEGV). In other minimized examples the same flaw could produce other “anything can happen” behavior, because once you jump to nonsense code, the machine is no longer executing the intended program.

Why would a compiler ever put “empty” into a vtable? The key is that Rust’s compiler aggressively proves which code paths are possible. If it concludes that a certain method can never be called for a particular trait object (because its requirements can never be satisfied), it may treat that method as unreachable and omit generating a real function pointer, leaving a “vacant” slot. Normally, that’s safe only if the method truly is impossible to call.

Here, the compiler’s reasoning went wrong. The issue was triggered by a complicated mix of generics, type constraints, and “hidden” types produced by `async` functions (and similar constructs that return opaque, unnamed types). In Rust 1.98, a change related to the “next trait solver” (an internal engine for answering “does this type satisfy this requirement?”) affected a check called “impossible predicates.” During a late compilation phase (post-analysis/code generation), the solver sometimes evaluated these requirements in the wrong “typing mode,” making it incorrectly decide that certain requirements were impossible. That mistaken conclusion then caused the vtable entry to be left null.

The fix was not to change user code, but to correct the compiler’s bookkeeping: if, during late compilation, the solver encounters these opaque/hidden types under certain conditions, it must *rerun* the evaluation using the original typing mode where the opaque types are handled correctly. A Rust PR (#158993) implemented this rerun rule more completely. Although it first landed on nightly/beta, it missed the Rust 1.98 release cutoff, so stable 1.98 shipped with the bug. The Rust team then backported the fix into a patch release, Rust 1.98.1 (#161555), and added tests to ensure vtables are no longer generated with bogus vacant method slots in this scenario.

</div>

<div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

In Rust, a `dyn Trait` value is a *fat pointer*: it contains

1) a pointer to the concrete object, and  
2) a pointer to a **vtable** (“virtual method table”) that holds function pointers for calling the trait’s methods (plus metadata like drop glue, size, alignment).

When you call a method through a trait object (dynamic dispatch), Rust does something morally like:

```text
fn_ptr = vtable[method_slot];
fn_ptr(data_ptr, ...args...)
```

So if the compiler ever emits a vtable where a required method slot is **null (0)**, a perfectly safe Rust call through `dyn Trait` will jump to address 0 and crash (SIGSEGV), or do other “impossible” things depending on optimization.

That’s exactly what happened in Rust 1.98.0.

---

## What went wrong in 1.98.0

The report showed:

- The vtable entries for **drop/size/alignment** were valid.
- But the first method entry (at offset `0x18`, i.e., 24 bytes after the start on that platform) was **zero**.
- Safe code performed a trait-object call, loaded the method pointer from the vtable, got `0`, and branched to it → **pc = 0** → segfault.

This was not “user UB”. It was a **miscompilation**: safe Rust triggered a crash because the compiler produced an invalid vtable.

---

## Why would rustc put a “vacant” slot in a vtable?

Internally, rustc can decide that some trait method implementation is **impossible** for a given type because the required *where-clause predicates* can’t be satisfied. There is a concept like “this vtable entry is *vacant*” (unreachable) if the solver proves the method can never actually be called.

That’s only sound if it’s truly impossible. If the compiler is wrong, you get a vtable with a missing method pointer even though the call can happen at runtime.

In this bug, rustc’s reasoning went wrong during compilation of certain complex generic/async-heavy code patterns (the Rama “boxed async service” setup was a real-world trigger; later a tiny reproducer showed it could happen with a much smaller generic setup).

---

## The key “why now?”: next-solver + typing modes + opaques

Two pieces of background:

### 1) `impl Trait` / async fn produce **opaque types**
An `async fn` returns an anonymous state-machine type. In type system terms, that’s an **opaque type** (similar to `impl Trait`). These opaques can be treated differently depending on compilation phase.

### 2) rustc uses different **TypingMode**s
Rust evaluates trait predicates in different “modes” depending on context (type checking, coherence, codegen/post-analysis, etc.). Some modes treat opaques as “erased/hidden”, others “revealed”.

The regression was introduced by work around “rigid aliases” and solver behavior (PR #156742). Then, in the problematic path, the compiler did a trait/predicate evaluation in **PostAnalysis/Codegen typing mode** and encountered opaques (from `async fn` / `impl Sized` / etc.). In that mode, it could end up:

- deciding certain predicates are “impossible” (because it compared a *rigid* opaque/alias to a revealed concrete type, or otherwise failed to relate terms), and therefore
- concluding a trait object method could never be called, and therefore
- producing a vtable slot as “vacant” → encoded as **0**.

But later, code generation still emitted a dynamic dispatch call through that method slot, because from the language point of view the trait object *does* have that method.

Result: safe code calls through a null function pointer.

---

## Why it only affected stable 1.98 even though “next-solver” is experimental

The subtlety is that even on stable, some compiler subsystems (notably things around *coherence* and “impossible predicates” checks) may use the newer solver machinery to prove things like “this impl can never apply” or “this predicate is uncallable”.

So a next-solver bug can leak into stable as “the compiler now believes something is impossible” and uses that belief to optimize/construct artifacts like vtables.

That’s what happened here.

---

## The fix (and why it works)

A PR that already existed on nightly, #158993, changed the solver behavior:

> **If we hit opaques during post-analysis/codegen evaluation, rerun the evaluation in the original typing mode.**

In other words: don’t make final “impossible / impossible_predicates” decisions in a typing mode where opaques are treated too opaquely or too rigidly; instead, *rerun* in a mode where the solver can see enough to make a correct decision.

Rust 1.98.0 had a case where it reran for one opaque-related condition but **not** for a combined condition:
`OpaqueInStorageOrAnyOpaqueHasInferAsHidden`. That missing rerun path is what let the wrong “impossible” conclusion slip through.

The 1.98.1 patch (backport PR #161555) changed:

- In `TypingMode::PostAnalysis | TypingMode::Codegen`, for that combined opaque condition, the rerun decision became **Yes** instead of **No**.

With that rerun, rustc no longer incorrectly concludes “this method is impossible”, so it emits a normal vtable entry pointing at the method, and the crash disappears.

---

## Why the workaround helped

The workaround in Rama effectively changed where the type-erasure boundary was:

- Instead of erasing a complex generic `Service` into a boxed trait object right where those tricky predicates/opaques were involved,
- it moved to a simpler erased shape (like `Arc<dyn Fn(Request) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<...>>>>`) or used manual dispatch via `Any` + function pointer.

That reduces the compiler’s need to solve complicated predicates at the exact trait-object-vtable construction point, avoiding the buggy “impossible” determination in 1.98.0.

---

## Bottom line

- Rust 1.98.0 could miscompile certain programs by generating a **trait-object vtable with a null method pointer**.
- The null happened because the compiler incorrectly decided a method was “impossible” due to a **solver/typing-mode bug involving opaque (`impl Trait` / async) types** during post-analysis/codegen predicate evaluation.
- Calling that method through `dyn Trait` in safe code then jumped to address 0 (or caused other UB-like behavior under optimization).
- Rust 1.98.1 fixed it by ensuring those cases **rerun in the correct typing mode**, preventing the incorrect “impossible predicate” and thus preventing the vacant vtable slot.

</div>

# The Vacant Vtable Bug: A Tale of Compiler Optimization Gone Wrong

In August 2026, developers using Rust version 1.98.0 encountered a serious bug that caused their programs to crash unexpectedly. The bug was particularly problematic because it affected a production web framework called Rama, breaking its continuous integration system with every commit.

## What Went Wrong

The bug caused programs to crash with a segmentation fault—essentially trying to access memory at address zero, which is never valid. In simpler terms, the program was trying to jump to a nonexistent location and execute instructions that weren't there. This manifested as immediate crashes, and in some cases, even more unpredictable behavior due to the undefined nature of the error.

The problem specifically affected code using "boxed async services"—a pattern for writing web services where different implementations can be swapped at runtime. When Rust compiled this code, it created what's called a "vtable" (virtual table)—a lookup table that helps the program find the correct function to call when dealing with these interchangeable implementations.

The critical error was that Rust 1.98.0 was creating vtables with empty slots where actual function addresses should have been. When the program tried to call a function through this table, it found zero instead of a valid memory address, causing an immediate crash.

## Why It Happened

The root cause lay in improvements made to Rust's type system solver—the component that figures out how different types relate to each other and whether code is valid. In May 2026, developers added a feature called "rigid aliases" to help the compiler avoid unnecessary work when analyzing types that couldn't be simplified further.

However, this optimization introduced a subtle problem. The compiler would sometimes incorrectly conclude that certain function implementations couldn't possibly exist under specific conditions. When generating the vtable, it would then leave those "impossible" slots empty rather than filling them with the actual function addresses.

The bug went unnoticed during development because it only affected specific combinations of features: async functions, trait objects (Rust's mechanism for runtime polymorphism), and particular patterns of type relationships. It passed through beta testing and made it into the stable 1.98.0 release.

## The Fix

Fortunately, a separate fix had already been developed in July 2026 for a related issue. That fix addressed how the compiler handled "opaque types"—types whose full definition is intentionally hidden—in different analysis modes. The key insight was that when the compiler encountered these opaque types during code generation, it needed to re-evaluate its decisions using different rules.

When developers realized that this July fix would have prevented the August crashes, they quickly backported it to the stable release. Within two weeks of the initial report, Rust 1.98.1 was released with the fix included.

The resolution demonstrates both the challenges of modern compiler development—where optimizations can have unexpected interactions—and the effectiveness of the Rust community's response system. By running comprehensive test suites against beta releases and maintaining careful tracking of related issues, the team was able to identify, diagnose, and fix a subtle but serious bug relatively quickly.

<div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

# The Vacant Vtable Bug in Rust 1.98

## What Happened

Rust 1.98.0 contained a compiler bug that caused certain programs to **segfault at address zero** - essentially crashing by trying to execute code at memory location 0x00000000. This is a serious miscompilation where the compiler generated incorrect code that caused undefined behavior in otherwise safe Rust programs.

The bug manifested when using complex trait objects with async functions and associated type bounds. The compiler would generate a **vtable** (virtual function table) with a **zero/null entry** where a valid function pointer should be. When the program tried to call that method through dynamic dispatch, it would jump to address zero and crash.

## What's a Vtable?

When you use trait objects in Rust (like `&dyn Trait`), the compiler needs to support **dynamic dispatch** - calling methods when the concrete type isn't known at compile time. It does this using a vtable: a table of function pointers specific to each concrete type implementing the trait.

For example:
```rust
trait Animal {
    fn speak(&self);
}

// When you have &dyn Animal, the vtable contains:
// - pointer to drop function
// - size and alignment info  
// - pointer to the actual speak() implementation
```

## The Bug

In Rust 1.98, under specific circumstances involving:
- Trait objects with associated types
- Associated type bounds (like `BodyError: Sized`)
- Async functions or opaque return types (`impl Trait`)
- Complex trait relationships

The compiler would emit a vtable entry containing **zero** instead of a valid function pointer. When code tried to call that method, the CPU would attempt to jump to address 0x0 and crash.

From the crash report:
```
PC (program counter): 0x0000000000000000  
LR (link register): points to the call site
```

The program counter at zero confirms execution jumped to a null pointer.

## Root Cause

The bug was introduced by PR #156742, which added a "rigid alias marker" to optimize type normalization in Rust's next-generation trait solver. The issue involved **typing modes** - different contexts where the compiler evaluates types:

1. **Analysis mode**: Used during type checking
2. **Post-analysis/Codegen mode**: Used when generating code

The bug occurred when evaluating trait bounds in post-analysis mode with opaque types (like the return type of `async fn`). The compiler would:

1. Start evaluating whether a type implements a trait
2. Encounter an opaque type and set a flag to "rerun this check"
3. Combine multiple rerun conditions in a way that **cancelled out the rerun**
4. Conclude (incorrectly) that the trait bound was impossible to satisfy
5. Emit a `VtblEntry::Vacant` marker - essentially saying "this method can never be called"

But the method *could* be called, leading to the crash.

## The Fix

PR #158993 fixed the issue by ensuring that when certain rerun conditions are met during post-analysis mode, the evaluation **does** rerun in the original typing mode:

```rust
// Before (buggy):
(RerunCondition::OpaqueInStorageOrAnyOpaqueHasInferAsHidden(_),
 TypingMode::PostAnalysis | TypingMode::Codegen) 
    => RerunDecision::No,  // ❌ Don't rerun

// After (fixed):
(RerunCondition::OpaqueInStorageOrAnyOpaqueHasInferAsHidden(_),
 TypingMode::PostAnalysis | TypingMode::Codegen)
    => RerunDecision::Yes, // ✅ Do rerun
```

This one-word change (`No` → `Yes`) fixed the miscompilation.

## Why It Matters

This bug is notable because:

1. **It affected stable Rust** (1.98.0) - not just experimental features
2. **It could cause silent miscompilation** beyond just crashes (LLVM could optimize based on the assumption that the null pointer was unreachable)
3. **It bypassed Rust's safety guarantees** - safe code crashed with undefined behavior
4. **It was caught quickly** by a user's CI running comprehensive tests

<div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

Rust’s compiler had a bug in version 1.98.0 that could make certain perfectly valid programs crash at runtime. The problem affected programs using “trait objects”—a way of storing different kinds of objects behind one common interface—and was especially likely when the interface represented an asynchronous service.

A useful analogy is a telephone directory. A trait object contains both the actual object and a small table of instructions describing how to call its methods. This table is called a *vtable*. When the program asks the object to perform an operation, it looks up the appropriate entry in the table and jumps to the machine-code address recorded there.

In this bug, Rust generated the table but left one method entry empty—literally a zero address. The program then performed an ordinary, safe method call. At the machine-code level, that meant attempting to execute code at address zero, producing a segmentation fault. Depending on optimization and surrounding code, the invalid entry could also lead to other undefined behavior, such as illegal instructions or incorrect results.

The affected programs tended to have several features at once: generic service types, nested trait implementations, asynchronous functions or hidden compiler-generated future types, and conversion to a dynamically dispatched service. The Rama proxy application in the report matched this pattern. When an upstream connection failed, the proxy should have returned an HTTP 502 response and continued running. Instead, its dynamically dispatched service call used the empty vtable entry and crashed.

The immediate cause was a change introduced in Rust 1.98 while improving the compiler’s “next trait solver,” the part of the compiler that determines whether types satisfy generic requirements. Another change had introduced “rigid aliases,” which are internal representations used for types whose exact details are intentionally hidden. Asynchronous functions commonly produce such hidden types: an `async fn` does not expose the concrete type of its future.

During a later compiler phase—after most type checking was complete—the solver sometimes encountered one of these hidden types while evaluating whether a generic condition was possible. It evaluated the condition in a context where the hidden type was not being interpreted correctly. The solver consequently decided that a required method implementation was impossible, even though it was valid. The vtable generator trusted that conclusion and marked the method slot as vacant instead of emitting the real method pointer.

This was a compiler miscompilation, not an error in the application. The program used safe Rust, and the compiler should never generate an invalid vtable for it.

The underlying fix was to make the solver retry these evaluations in the original typing context whenever hidden types appeared during post-analysis or code generation. That retry allows the compiler to reveal and interpret the relevant opaque type correctly, find the valid implementation, and place its address in the vtable.

The fix had already appeared in the development compiler, but it missed the Rust 1.98 release because of the beta-release timing. Rust 1.98.1 backported the correction, added a regression test based on this failure, and documented the release as fixing a miscompilation in vtable generation. Updating to 1.98.1 removes the need for the reported workarounds.

</div>

<div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

## What went wrong

This was a **rustc miscompilation**, not an error in Rama’s use of boxed services or async traits.

Rama uses a common pattern for dynamic dispatch of an async service:

1. A concrete service implements a trait such as `Service`.
2. The service is erased behind a trait object.
3. Calling the service goes through a compiler-generated vtable.
4. The async result is boxed as a `Future`.

Conceptually, the vtable looked like this:

```text
+--------------------+
| drop function      |
| object size        |
| object alignment   |
| Service::serve ptr |  <-- should be a function pointer
+--------------------+
```

With Rust 1.98.0, rustc generated a vtable where the final entry was zero:

```text
Service::serve ptr = 0
```

The generated caller then performed an indirect call through that entry. On macOS, that meant branching to address zero and segfaulting.

The source code remained entirely safe Rust. The problem was that rustc generated an invalid vtable.

---

## Why was the method slot considered “vacant”?

The affected implementation was a generic or blanket implementation whose applicability involved several predicates, projections, and opaque types.

The minimized example has roughly this structure:

```rust
impl<F, R, ResBody> Trait for (F, PhantomData<R>)
where
    F: Fn() -> R,
    HttpClientService: Service<Output = ResBody>,
    ResBody: StreamingBody<BodyError: Sized>,
{
    fn method(&self) {}
}
```

The actual type was valid and the implementation was applicable. However, determining whether a vtable entry should be emitted requires rustc to prove that the implementation and its method are usable for the relevant erased type.

During code generation, rustc’s next-generation trait solver incorrectly concluded that the predicates were impossible. In effect, it reasoned:

> “This implementation cannot exist for this type, so its vtable method can be vacant.”

That conclusion was false.

A “vacant” vtable entry is useful internally when rustc has proven that a method cannot be called for a particular trait-object configuration. But in this case the solver’s false result leaked into code generation, and rustc emitted a zero function pointer for a method that was actually callable.

---

## Why did async code or `impl Trait` matter?

The important factor was not specifically Tokio, futures, or Rama.

Async functions and `impl Trait` introduce **opaque types**. For example:

```rust
async fn inspect() {}
```

has an implicitly generated, hidden future type. Similarly:

```rust
fn inspect() -> impl Sized { ... }
```

has a hidden return type.

Those opaque types participated in the trait-solver query, even when the type was not obviously relevant to the method body. The bug was triggered by the interaction of:

- an opaque type from `async fn` or `impl Trait`,
- generic predicates and associated-type projections,
- a blanket trait implementation,
- trait-object/vtable generation,
- the next-generation trait solver’s post-analysis behavior.

That is why removing the async function or replacing it with a sufficiently simple concrete type could make the issue disappear.

It also explains why the bug appeared in one particular boxed-service location rather than in every use of `BoxService`: this was a very specific combination of type-system features.

---

## The regression

The problematic behavior was introduced by rust-lang/rust#156742, which added support for **rigid aliases**.

Rigid aliases are part of the machinery used by the next-generation trait solver to represent types whose aliases should not be normalized in the current typing environment. The change was correct in isolation, but it exposed an incomplete case in later solver logic.

The relevant failure occurred when rustc was evaluating predicates in a post-analysis or code-generation typing mode. If it encountered an opaque type in a form that depended on the original typing mode, it sometimes reused an incorrect result instead of reevaluating the predicate in the appropriate mode.

That produced a false “impossible predicate” result.

The issue was therefore approximately:

```text
opaque type encountered
        ↓
predicate evaluated in the wrong typing mode
        ↓
false “impossible” result
        ↓
vtable method marked vacant
        ↓
zero function pointer emitted
        ↓
safe dynamic dispatch jumps to address 0
```

The minimized example was especially valuable because it showed that the issue did not require the full Rama dependency graph.

---

## The fix

Rust PR #158993 changed the solver so that, when this particular opaque-type situation is encountered during post-analysis or code generation, rustc **reruns the evaluation in the original typing mode** instead of trusting the incorrect result.

The important behavioral change was effectively:

```diff
- do not rerun
+ rerun in the original typing mode
```

That allowed rustc to see the real, valid implementation and generate the proper `Trait::method` function pointer in the vtable.

The fix landed after the Rust 1.98 beta cutoff, so Rust 1.98.0 was released with the bug while newer nightlies already contained the correction. It was then backported in Rust 1.98.1 via PR #161555.

Rust 1.98.1 also added a regression test based on the minimized reproducer.

---

## Why the workaround helped

The Rama workaround changed the dispatch boundary so that the generic `Service` predicate was handled outside the problematic erased trait-object call.

For example, replacing a custom erased async trait with an `Arc<dyn Fn(...) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<...>>>>` meant that rustc no longer had to generate the same complicated vtable for the generic service implementation.

The alternative workaround stored:

- the service as an ordinary erased `Any` value, and
- a concrete monomorphized function pointer for dispatch.

That also avoided the faulty custom vtable entry. It was not fixing an invalid abstraction in Rama; it was routing around the compiler bug.

---

## Bottom line

- Rama’s code was valid safe Rust.
- Rust 1.98.0 incorrectly decided that a valid trait method was unavailable.
- It generated a trait-object vtable with a null method pointer.
- Dynamic dispatch called that pointer and crashed.
- The root cause was an interaction between the next-generation trait solver, opaque types, and post-analysis typing modes.
- Rust 1.98.1 backported the fix from #158993 and corrected the vtable generation.
- The correct remedy for users was upgrading to **Rust 1.98.1 or later**, rather than changing the service abstraction.

</div>

<div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

Think of a program’s “call me” list as a little phone book. For features that are chosen at runtime (Rust calls them trait objects), the compiler builds a tiny table, a vtable, that lists which number to dial for each method. When your code says “call the method,” the processor looks up the number in that table and jumps there.

In Rust 1.98, the compiler sometimes wrote a vtable with a blank entry for a real method. When the program later tried to call through that blank entry, the processor jumped to address zero — which on modern systems is invalid — and the program crashed (a segfault). On some builds it could also misbehave in other ways (UB: undefined behavior), like illegal-instruction traps or even wrong logic, because the optimizer may assume “calling through a null pointer never happens” and rearrange code accordingly.

Why did the compiler leave that slot blank? It made a wrong “this can never happen” decision while reasoning about types. Recent Rust compilers use a sophisticated “trait solver” — a logic engine that answers questions like “under these conditions, does this type really provide that method?” To speed and structure this reasoning, the solver sometimes looks at types in different “modes,” and it treats some details as temporarily hidden “opaques” (for example, the hidden return type of an async function). A June change (adding a “rigid alias” marker) made the solver hold on to some of these hidden forms more firmly.

Here’s where the bug appeared: during a late compilation phase (post-analysis/code generation), if the solver bumped into certain opaque details while checking whether a method’s preconditions could ever be met, it was supposed to say, “I might be looking with blurry glasses; rerun this check in the original, clearer mode.” In one combined case — signaled internally as “OpaqueInStorageOrAnyOpaqueHasInferAsHidden” — that rerun didn’t happen. The solver then incorrectly concluded, “this method’s conditions are impossible,” and told the vtable builder to mark the entry as vacant. The code still tried to call it, and boom.

This slipped into stable 1.98 because even though the “next” solver is still being rolled out, one stable pass (impossible_predicates) already uses it to decide which vtable slots to fill. So a solver mistake there directly miscompiled binaries.

It was most visible in a real project (Rama) that uses a popular pattern: boxing an async “service” behind a trait object and calling it dynamically. The same code worked on 1.97.1, crashed on 1.98.0, and worked again on a recent nightly and on beta — a strong sign of a compiler regression.

The fix was straightforward once identified: whenever that specific opaque-related condition occurs in the late phase, always rerun the check in the original typing mode. That forces the solver to “take off the blurry glasses,” reveal enough about the opaque types, and avoid the false “impossible” conclusion. This change (PR #158993) was already in nightly/beta and was backported to 1.98.1 (PR #161555), along with tests that recreate the scenario to prevent regressions.

In the meantime, the reporter found workarounds (rewriting code to avoid that erased async-vtable boundary), but with 1.98.1 released, users should simply upgrade. The episode is a reminder that miscompilations can be subtle, and that running real-world test suites on beta helps catch rare but impactful issues early.

</div>

<div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

Short version

- In Rust 1.98, the compiler could generate a trait-object vtable whose first method pointer was zero.
- Safe Rust then did a dynamic call through that pointer and jumped to address 0 → segfault/UB.
- This happened when building vtables for certain “boxed async service” style trait objects, i.e. the common “async fn in trait” erasure pattern that returns Pin&lt;Box&lt;dyn Future&lt;…>>>.
- Root cause: a bug in the “next trait solver” path used while deciding which methods to put in a vtable. It wrongly concluded a method’s where-clauses were impossible, marked the vtable slot as “vacant,” and wrote 0 there.
- Fixed in 1.98.1 and later (also fixed on beta/nightly earlier). Upgrade your toolchain.

What’s a vtable and how can it be wrong?

- A trait object like Box&lt;dyn Trait> points to:
  - data pointer (the object)
  - vtable pointer (type-erased metadata): drop fn, size, align, then one function pointer per trait method.
- Dynamic dispatch loads the function pointer from the vtable and calls it.
- If a vtable entry is 0, that’s undefined behavior when called (you’ll usually crash).

Why would the compiler ever write a “vacant” vtable slot?

- Rust tries to omit vtable entries the program can prove will never be called at runtime. It uses a solver to check if the method’s extra bounds (“predicates”) can ever hold for the erased receiver type. If the predicates are provably impossible, the method is treated as unreachable and the entry can be marked “vacant.”
- That’s sound only if the solver’s answer (“impossible”) is correct. If it’s wrong, you get a null entry and a crash in safe code.

What broke in 1.98?

- 1.98 included internal changes to the “next trait solver” (PR #156742 adds “rigid aliases”). The next solver is used in a few places on stable (notably the “impossible predicates” check used while assembling vtables).
- “Async” and “impl Trait” introduce opaque types (hidden concrete types). The solver runs in different “typing modes.” In some modes opaques are kept rigid/opaque; in others they can be “revealed” to their hidden type so relations can be proven.
- The solver is supposed to say “I hit an opaque here; please rerun this query in the original typing mode” in certain cases.
- Bug: one combination of “rerun” conditions (OpaqueInStorageOrAnyOpaqueHasInferAsHidden) in PostAnalysis/Codegen mode didn’t actually trigger that rerun. The solver then incorrectly concluded a method’s predicates were impossible.
- Result: rustc decided a vtable method “can never be called,” put a Vacant entry (0) into the vtable, and generated no code for the real method. At runtime, the program performed a dynamic call through that slot and branched to 0.

Why did “async” or “impl Trait” seem load‑bearing?

- They create these opaque (“impl Trait”) types the solver must sometimes “reveal.” If it stays opaque in the wrong mode, goals that should succeed can look impossible.
- That’s why a tiny example like “a function returning impl Sized” or “async fn” could still reproduce the issue.

Symptoms you might have seen

- On aarch64-apple-darwin (and elsewhere): SIGSEGV at pc=0 during a dyn call.
- In optimized builds, you might also see SIGILL or subtler misbehavior: it’s UB, so LLVM is allowed to make aggressive assumptions.
- Debug with opt-level=0 often crashes cleanly; with opt-level>0 behavior can vary.

Workarounds people used (not needed after 1.98.1)

- Avoid relying on the compiler-generated vtable entry for the custom “async-erased” trait:
  - Store an Arc&lt;dyn Any> plus an explicit function pointer that knows how to downcast and call; or
  - Replace the boxed service with Arc&lt;dyn Fn(Input) -> Pin&lt;Box&lt;dyn Future&lt;…>>> + Send + Sync>.
- These sidestep the compiler’s “impossible predicates” pruning for that vtable method.

Fix and versions

- Fixed by PR #158993 (“rerun in original typing mode if we meet any opaques in post analysis”), which teaches the solver to rerun for the missing condition.
- Backported in Rust 1.98.1 (PR #161555). Also present in 1.99 beta and recent nightlies.
- Action: upgrade to 1.98.1 or newer if you saw crashes/regressions in 1.98.0.

Why only some code hit it?

- The bug needed a specific puzzle piece combo: a trait-object method whose predicates depend on an opaque type introduced by async/impl Trait, assessed by the next solver in a mode where opaques stayed rigid, and the missed rerun path.
- Many boxed trait objects don’t trip that exact path, so you might only see it in one corner of a codebase.

Takeaway

- This was a miscompilation that produced UB in safe Rust by emitting a null vtable method pointer under rare but real conditions involving async/impl Trait and dynamic dispatch.
- It’s fixed in 1.98.1+. If you must stay on 1.98.0, use one of the manual-erasure workarounds, but upgrading is strongly recommended.

</div>

In August 2026, a Rust developer noticed that a networking program which had worked fine for years suddenly began crashing the moment he rebuilt it with the newest version of the Rust compiler (1.98). To understand what went wrong, it helps to know one idea from how compiled programs work. Sometimes a program deals with an object whose exact type isn't known until the program is running. To handle this, the compiler builds a small lookup table for each such object, a kind of directory listing where each of the object's methods lives in memory. When the program needs to call a method, it looks up the entry in the directory and jumps there. In this bug, the compiler had filled in most of the directory correctly, but left one entry blank, a zero. When the program looked up that method and jumped, it jumped to nowhere.

Why would a compiler leave an entry blank on purpose? Rust's compiler has a legitimate feature for this. Some methods come with conditions attached ("this only works if the input type can be sorted," say), and if the compiler can prove those conditions can *never* be satisfied for a particular type, it knows the method can never be called. Rather than generate useless code, it leaves the slot empty. This is safe as long as the compiler's proof is correct.

The proof was wrong. Deciding whether conditions can be satisfied is the job of a component called the trait solver, and Rust has been gradually replacing its old solver with a new one. In May 2026, a large change to the new solver was merged (adding "rigidness markers," an internal optimization about when the compiler can trust it has fully simplified a type). That change introduced a subtle flaw: in a specific late stage of compilation, when the solver encountered a certain kind of placeholder type (produced by asynchronous functions, among other things), it was supposed to re-check its reasoning under different rules, but a decision table said "no, don't re-check." Skipping that step caused the solver to wrongly conclude that the method's conditions were impossible. So it left the slot blank, and it did so silently, without the error message a compiler normally produces when confused.

The flaw was actually discovered and fixed in July, about two weeks after it was introduced, by a developer who hit an internal compiler crash while building a different project. The fix was tiny: one word in a decision table changed from "No" to "Yes." But Rust releases work like trains on a schedule. The bug had boarded the train for version 1.98 before the fix arrived, and nobody noticed that the two were separated by that cutoff. So 1.98 shipped with the bug but not the fix, while the following version had both.

Once the report came in, volunteers narrowed the crash from a large networking library down to a 30-line example, pinpointed the exact commit that caused it, and confirmed the July fix cured it. The Rust team judged this serious enough for an emergency patch release. Version 1.98.1, containing the one-word fix and two new regression tests, shipped on September 3, two weeks after the report. The reporter added a daily test run against pre-release compilers so future problems of this kind could be caught before they reach the public.

</div>

<h3 id="anthropic--claude-fable-5-1--run-2">Run 2: rank 29, 77/100</h3>

<p>understanding 34/40 · accuracy 21/30 · accessibility 17/20 · calibration 5/10<br>1273 words · 3,132 output tokens (158 reported as reasoning) · effort: adaptive, high</p>

<div class="explainer-flag"><p><strong>Model errors about a real person</strong>: claims the thread does not support.</p><ul><li>“Adwin White found the same missing rerun”: the thread names the author of the fix only by the GitHub handle adwinwhite.</li><li>“bjorn3 correctly guessed #158993 from memory”: the thread shows bjorn3 asking whether #158993 could have fixed it, not how bjorn3 came to it.</li></ul></div>

<div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

## The short version

Rust 1.98.0 shipped with a compiler bug that could produce a **vtable with a null pointer in a method slot**. Calling that method through `dyn Trait` jumped to address zero and segfaulted. There was nothing wrong with the user's code; the compiler simply decided, incorrectly, that a perfectly valid trait method could never be called, and left its slot empty. The fix was a one-line change to the trait solver, released as 1.98.1.

## What a "vacant" vtable slot is and why it exists

When you coerce a `&T` into a `&dyn Trait`, rustc builds a vtable: drop glue, size, alignment, then one function pointer per method. But not every method in a trait can actually be called for every implementing type. Consider:

```rust
trait Trait {
    fn method(&self) where Self: Copy;
}
```

If `T` isn't `Copy`, there's no valid instantiation of `method` for `T`, and the compiler is not allowed to emit one. Rather than fail, rustc writes `VtblEntry::Vacant` — a null — into that slot, reasoning that safe code can never reach it. To make this decision it runs a query called `impossible_predicates` over the method's `where`-clauses. If the solver says "these can never hold," the slot is left empty.

That decision is only sound if the solver is *right*. Here it wasn't.

## The minimized trigger

theemathas whittled the multi-crate failure down to this:

```rust
impl<F, R, ResBody> Trait for (F, PhantomData<R>)
where
    F: Fn() -> R,
    HttpClientService: Service<Output = ResBody>,
    ResBody: StreamingBody<BodyError: Sized>,
{
    fn method(&self) {}
}

async fn inspect_websocket_message() {}

fn main() {
    (&(inspect_websocket_message, PhantomData) as &dyn Trait).method();
}
```

Every bound is satisfiable: `HttpClientService::Output` is `Body`, `Body::BodyError` is `MyError`, which is `Sized`. Yet 1.98.0 concluded the predicates were impossible and emitted a null for `method`. Notice the `async fn` (or equivalently, a function returning `impl Sized`). The "load-bearing" ingredient is that `R` ends up being an **opaque type** — the anonymous future / `impl Trait` — that appears inside the trait-solving problem. That's the thread to pull on.

## Why the solver got it wrong

Two facts collide here:

**1. `impossible_predicates` already uses the new trait solver.** Rust's "next solver" isn't the default for typechecking yet, but a few pieces of the compiler — coherence and this vtable query — already route through it. So a new-solver bug that seems safely behind a `-Znext-solver` flag can leak onto stable through these back doors. lcnr says exactly this in the 1.98.1 PR: "it's easy to forget that we need to be careful with next-solver bugs as they can affect stable via coherence and `impossible_predicates`."

**2. Opaque types behave differently depending on *typing mode*.** During ordinary analysis, `impl Trait` is treated as an abstract "rigid" type — you can only use what its bounds promise. After analysis (in `PostAnalysis`/`Codegen` mode), it's revealed to be its concrete hidden type. The solver sometimes evaluates a goal, notices partway through that it made assumptions about opaques that would come out differently in another mode, and records a **rerun condition**: "if this answer matters, re-evaluate me in the original mode."

The regressing PR, #156742, added a "rigid alias" marker so the solver could skip renormalizing aliases it already knew were rigid. That reshuffled enough of the machinery that an existing gap in the rerun logic became reachable. Here's the relevant table, before the fix:

```rust
(RerunCondition::OpaqueInStorage, PostAnalysis | Codegen) => Yes,
(RerunCondition::OpaqueInStorageOrAnyOpaqueHasInferAsHidden(_), PostAnalysis | Codegen) => No,   // bug
```

There are two separate reasons a goal might need rerunning: an opaque ended up in the solver's storage, or an opaque got an inference variable as its hidden type. When *both* happen, they merge into the combined condition. Someone had correctly said "rerun" for the first flag alone but written "don't rerun" for the combined case — an oversight, not a design decision.

Walk through what happened with the reproducer in `Codegen` mode:

- The solver tries to prove the `where`-clauses. Along the way it instantiates impls with fresh inference variables (setting the "infer as hidden" flag) and encounters the opaque return type of `inspect_websocket_message` (setting the "opaque in storage" flag).
- Because it's in a mode where the opaque is treated as rigid, some intermediate relation between the opaque and its revealed type fails.
- The failure comes back tagged `OpaqueInStorageOrAnyOpaqueHasInferAsHidden`, which *should* mean "this failure isn't trustworthy — try again with opaques revealed."
- The table said `RerunDecision::No`. The failure was accepted as final.
- `impossible_predicates` returned `true`. The method's vtable slot was left null.

Nothing errored, nothing warned. The program compiled and then jumped to address zero the first time it hit that dynamic call.

## Why it was already fixed on nightly but broken on stable

Adwin White found the same missing rerun about two weeks after #156742 landed, while building `cargo` with the new solver (it ICE'd rather than miscompiling there), and fixed it in #158993 by flipping `No` to `Yes`. Nobody connected that fix to a stable-visible miscompilation, and — crucially — a beta cutoff had happened between the regression and the fix. So 1.98 branched with the bug, nightly moved on without it, and GlenDC's bisection produced the confusing "broken in 1.98.0, fine in 1.97.1, fine again on nightly" pattern. That's also why theemathas's search for the "fixing" commit pointed at an unrelated rollup: the bisection tooling was confounded by the branch geometry, and bjorn3 correctly guessed #158993 from memory.

## Why it only showed up in one place in rama

The user's puzzlement is understandable — rama boxes services and does the "async fn in dyn trait" erasure dance all over the place. But the bug needs a specific conjunction: a trait object whose method's `where`-clauses involve *both* an opaque type (here, the future from an `async fn` passed through `service_fn`) *and* enough projection chasing (`Layer<...>::Service`, `Service<Output = ...>`, `StreamingBody<Error: Into<...>>`) that the solver instantiates impls with inference variables. Only the `EagerHttpProxyConnector` / `UpgradeService` path threaded an `async fn`-based service through that particular set of bounds. Both of GlenDC's workarounds worked for the same reason: they moved the generic `R: Service` predicate out of the erased method's `where`-clause so `impossible_predicates` never looked at it.

## On severity

lcnr initially described this as a "near guaranteed segfault," which is the benign face of it. But a null function pointer in a vtable is undefined behavior, not a reliable crash. theemathas demonstrated that with optimizations on, LLVM will happily reason from "this pointer is never null" and produce silently wrong control flow rather than a crash — in rama's case that was masked by `opt-level = 1` in the dev profile producing SIGILL and "future resumed after completion" panics. That's what justified a point release rather than waiting for 1.99.

## Takeaways

- **"Impossible predicate" analyses are soundness-critical.** Any place the compiler uses a "can this ever be true?" answer to elide code — vacant vtable slots, dead-branch elimination, coherence — turns a solver *incompleteness* bug (failing to prove something true) into a *miscompilation*. Most solver bugs just cause spurious type errors; these ones cause UB.
- **Feature flags don't fully contain a component that has partial callers.** The new solver being opt-in for typeck didn't protect stable, because two queries already depend on it unconditionally.
- **Fixes need to be triaged for backport, not just merged.** #158993 was framed as "fixes an ICE building cargo with -Znext-solver," which sounded nightly-only. It took a stable miscompile report to reveal it was a beta-critical fix that had already sailed past the cutoff. The regression test added in 1.98.1 is under `tests/ui/traits/object/` rather than `next-solver/` precisely to record that this path is stable-visible.

</div>

The nightly bisection was done by mProjectsCode, and the beta fix-bisection by theemathas.</li><li>"the bisection tooling was confounded by the branch geometry, and bjorn3 correctly guessed #158993 from memory" — the source only says the bisection pointed to #159293 and none of its PRs seemed relevant; no explanation for that is given. <div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

Imagine you have a directory of customer-service hotlines. Each service (billing, tech support, sales) gets a name and a phone number. When a call comes in, the receptionist looks up the requested service in that directory and dials the number. Now picture a printing error that leaves the “tech support” phone number blank. If the receptionist tries to dial that entry, they end up dialing “nothing,” which immediately fails.

That’s essentially what happened inside Rust 1.98.0. The Rust compiler creates a small “directory” (called a vtable) whenever code asks to call a component through a general interface rather than a specific implementation. One slot in this table is the address of the actual function to run. In this release, under a very particular combination of modern Rust features—calling an asynchronous service through a boxed trait object—the compiler sometimes printed a vtable where the function slot was zero instead of a real address. When the program later tried to call through that slot, it jumped to address zero and crashed (a segmentation fault). In other cases, because this is undefined behavior, it could look like other kinds of failures too.

Why did the compiler do that? The root cause was a subtle logic change in how Rust reasons about types and capabilities behind the scenes. Rust uses a powerful “trait solver” to prove whether a piece of code is valid: for example, “does this object really support the method I want to call?” A recent change introduced the idea of certain type placeholders being “rigid” in specific contexts, and also tweaked when the solver should re-check its assumptions. Combined with code paths that already use the newer solver for special checks, the compiler could convince itself that a method would never actually be needed in the final program. Concluding it was “impossible,” it didn’t generate the method’s code and left a blank in the vtable—like omitting the tech support number because a prior step wrongly decided no one could ever call it.

A key ingredient in this misjudgment was the presence of “opaque” types—the compiler intentionally hides the exact concrete type of some async and “impl Trait” constructs until the right phase. In Rust 1.98.0, if the solver encountered these opaques at a late stage (“post-analysis” or during code generation), it didn’t always rerun its reasoning in the original mode where those types would be revealed enough to make a sound decision. That’s how it reached the false “impossible” conclusion and emitted a vacant slot.

How was it fixed? The compiler was updated so that whenever it hits these opaque types in that late stage, it reruns the check in the original mode. Put simply: if the directory publisher notices it’s looking at a redacted entry, it goes back to the unredacted source before printing. With that rerun, the solver correctly sees that the method is indeed needed, generates it, and fills in the vtable slot with a proper address. This fix landed quickly on the development branch and was backported to a patch release, Rust 1.98.1. Users who hit the crash on 1.98.0 can update to 1.98.1 to resolve it.

In short: a sophisticated but brittle shortcut in the compiler’s reasoning caused it to omit a needed phone number. The patch teaches it to double-check when information is hidden, ensuring the number makes it into the directory and calls go through safely.

<div class="explainer-text" markdown="1">

Short version
- Rust 1.98 could generate a trait-object vtable that contains a zero in a method slot.
- Safe Rust then calls through that slot and jumps to address 0 → instant UB (often a segfault).
- It was triggered by certain async/impl Trait-heavy generics behind a boxed trait object.
- Fixed in 1.98.1 (and already OK on nightly/beta). Upgrade if you hit it.

What actually went wrong
- When you use a trait object (like Box&lt;dyn Service&lt;…>>), rustc builds a vtable: [drop, size, align, method_0, method_1, …].
- Rustc sometimes omits a method from a vtable if it proves the method’s where-clauses can never be satisfied (“impossible_predicates”). In that case it writes a special “vacant” entry in the table instead of a function pointer.
- In 1.98, a logic bug in the “next trait solver” (which stable rustc already uses internally for certain queries like impossible_predicates) incorrectly concluded that some methods were impossible when opaque types (“impl Trait”, including those produced by async fn) were involved.
- Root cause: a recent change (rigid aliases) made the solver keep some “impl Trait”/projection results as rigid in a late typing mode (post-analysis/codegen). If any opaque showed up, the solver should have rerun the evaluation in the original typing mode to re-normalize properly. For one combined condition (OpaqueInStorageOrAnyOpaqueHasInferAsHidden), 1.98 forgot to rerun. The solver then “proved” the method’s predicates impossible, so codegen emitted a vacant (null) vtable slot.
- Result: safe dynamic dispatch loaded the method pointer from the vtable, got 0, and branched to null. On different builds you could see SIGSEGV, SIGILL, or other UB-style misbehavior.

Why async/impl Trait seemed “load-bearing”
- Async fns and many combinators produce opaque types (impl Trait). The bug was in how those opaques were handled across typing modes.
- That’s why adding/removing async or changing a function to return an opaque closure could flip the behavior.

How it was fixed
- PR #158993 taught the solver to rerun in the original typing mode whenever it sees opaques under the combined “OpaqueInStorageOrAnyOpaqueHasInferAsHidden” condition too, not just under the narrower condition.
- That correction landed on nightly, was present in 1.99 beta, and was backported to 1.98.1 (PR #161555). The issue is closed as fixed.

Impact and symptoms
- Platform-agnostic; reproducible on multiple targets (original report on aarch64-apple-darwin).
- Often crashes at runtime when calling through a boxed trait object with async/impl Trait in the mix.
- Could also manifest as other UB outcomes in optimized builds (e.g., SIGILL, strange behavior).

Workarounds if you can’t upgrade immediately
- Restructure the dynamic boundary to avoid placing the generic/async predicate directly on the vtable-dispatched trait:
  - Wrap the async call in a closure and erase that closure type (store a Fn(...) -> Pin&lt;Box&lt;dyn Future&lt;…>>>), keeping the generic bound outside the trait object.
  - Or store a separate function pointer alongside an Arc&lt;dyn Any> and downcast internally, instead of relying on a custom async-erasure trait with a vtable method.
- These patterns avoid the specific “impossible_predicates on vtable method” path that triggered the bug.

What to do
- Update to Rust 1.98.1 or newer. That’s the definitive fix.

</div>
